anatomy.lede: A mature female is mostly cape: two long arms joined by a broad web that she can unfurl, roll up or cut loose.

hotspots.label: Web
hotspots.text: Sheets of webbing stretch between the long dorsal arms of the female. She unfurls them to look bigger when threatened.

hotspots.label: Dorsal arm
hotspots.text: Young blanket octopuses have been found with fragments of Portuguese man o' war tentacles stuck to the suckers of these upper arms.

hotspots.label: Shorter arm
hotspots.text: The other arms are short and lined with suckers, and are not joined by the web.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Plates like this one were drawn from females in the 19th century. Scientists did not meet a live male until 2002.

hotspots.label: Mantle
hotspots.text: The female stores the detached arms of males inside her mantle cavity until she is ready to fertilise her eggs.

body.lede: Male and female blanket octopuses are built for completely different lives, and their bodies show it.

systems.title: The most unequal pair
systems.text: Few large animals show a bigger size gap between the sexes. One idea is that big females can carry more eggs, while staying small lets males keep using stolen stinging tentacles, a defence that only works at small sizes.

systems.title: A detachable arm
systems.text: The male's third right arm, the hectocotylus, holds a sperm-filled pouch. When he is ready to mate, the pouch ruptures, he cuts the arm off and gives it to a female, who may store several from different males.

systems.title: A huge supply of eggs
systems.text: In a mature Mediterranean female, researchers estimated more than 105,000 oocytes (developing eggs).

genome.lede: No nuclear genome has been published for the blanket octopus. Most genetic work has used mitochondrial DNA to sort out which species is which.

findings.title: Mitochondrial genome
findings.text: Its complete mitochondrial genome is 16,015 base pairs long and holds 13 protein-coding genes, 2 rRNA genes and 22 tRNA genes.

findings.title: Two species, not one
findings.text: Genetic comparison of a Gulf of Mexico female with Pacific sequences suggests that blanket octopuses in the Pacific previously called T. violaceus are a separate species, T. gracilis.

mind.lede: Blanket octopuses live far out in the open ocean, so most of what is known comes from chance encounters.

studies.title: Armed with stingers
studies.text: Young blanket octopuses were found with many pieces of Portuguese man o' war tentacles attached to their upper arms, which they may use for attack and defence.

studies.title: The first living male
studies.text: Scientists encountered a live male for the first time, off the Great Barrier Reef, confirming how tiny males are compared with females.

studies.title: Dropping arms to save eggs
studies.text: A mature female found in the Gulf of Mexico showed evidence of autotomy, shedding parts of her body, as a way of protecting her egg mass.

survival.lede: With no seafloor to hide on, a blanket octopus defends itself by looking huge or carrying weapons it has stolen.

tactics.title: Unfurling the cape
tactics.text: When attacked, a female can roll up her web and then unfurl it, looking much larger and possibly scaring a predator away.

tactics.title: Cutting the cape loose
tactics.text: The web can tear away when a predator bites it, distracting the attacker while the octopus escapes.

tactics.title: Borrowed stingers
tactics.text: Males and females smaller than about 7 cm have been reported carrying man o' war tentacles. This defence works only at small sizes.

life.lede: Male and female lead very different lives. The male matures tiny and dies soon after mating, while the female keeps growing to lay a huge batch of eggs.

stages.name: Young octopus
stages.text: Small juveniles drift in the open ocean, where some carry pieces of man o' war tentacles for protection.

stages.name: Mating
stages.text: The male detaches his sperm-filled arm and hands it to the female. Sperm packets found in a still-maturing female suggest females may mate with several males before they are fully mature.

stages.name: Spawning
stages.text: The female lays more than 100,000 eggs, then retrieves the stored arm and spreads the sperm over the egg mass.
